👇
To bypass an HP printer block on non-branded cartridges, dismiss prompt messages like "OK" or "Continue" if they appear. Otherwise, perform a hard power reset, disable Cartridge Protection in the printer settings or HP Smart App, clean the metal contacts, or reinstall the third-party cartridges one at a time.

Troubleshooting Steps: Dismiss the message: Press OK, Continue, or No on the printer screen if the option is available; some models let you print after acknowledging the warning.

Power reset: Unplug the printer while it is turned on, wait 2 minutes, plug it back into a direct wall outlet, and turn it on.

Reinstall sequentially: Remove all cartridges, insert one third-party cartridge, turn the printer off and on, and add remaining cartridges one by one.Clean the contacts: Take out the cartridges and wipe the copper-colored electrical chips with a clean, lint-free cloth or cotton swab.

Disable Cartridge Protection: Go to the setup or preferences menu on your printer's display screen or via the HP Smart App and turn off Cartridge Protection or anti-fraud settings.

Turn off auto-updates: Prevent future lockouts by turning off automatic firmware updates in your printer settings or software companion.A visual guide showing how to change settings and handle hardware tricks to clear non-HP cartridge warnings:

I have a couple of HP printers and went through this issue. I had signed up for the instant ink plan until I became increasingly frustrated that the company, essentially, bricks your ink cartridges once you reach a certain page limit. It doesn’t matter if there’s still ink left in the cartridge. Since then, I simply purchased the ink. I’m not getting any messages that I’m using unauthorized cartridges, but I have noticed lately that non-HP ink does not seem to print is vividly as HP. This was not an issue before.

What’s clear to me is that HP is not making any money on the hardware, but they’re making a fortune on the ink; so they’re trying to convince customers that these ink plans give them a printer for “free.”  They’re not slick and people are waking up to this madness. 

I’m going to make the analogy here to Spotify or Apple Music. I understand going in that I don’t own any of the music saved into my library of those devices. I am leasing the music for as long as I pay for the subscription. But with a printer, I bought the hardware.  I therefore should be able to decide how I use that printer and what ink I install on it. The company already made its money from me on the product. To then require me to pay in perpetuity for the “right“ to use said product is outrageous. It is diabolical. The moment HP installs any kind of firmware update and attempts to claim/assert control over a product I purchased years ago is the very moment that I am no longer using HP printers. And that’s a shame because it’s adding to the ever-growing tonnage of electronic waste.

comments.text: IT Guy here, PSA DO NOT UPDATE your printers firmware, it is a blacklist for generic ink carts. Also if you do get blacklisted contact your ink supplier and see if they have a refund policy, or can send out a different set. Sometimes they can walk you though a firmware downgrade to get them working again. Most of the time they know they are playing a cat a mouse game with the printer companies. Better yet, get a laser if you don't print that often, or an ink jet tank system like the Mega Tanks or Eco tanks for ink, saves a lot and removed most of the DRM that cartridges come with. You absolutely do NOT have to sign up for a subscription service those are all OPTIONAL on every printer, HP is the most egregious about it with weird dark patterns built in to trick you into signing up. They can be alright for you but are hard to unenroll from once it's started. If you had ink and you enroll in these plans, your tossing the ink and buying genuine carts for at least your first time out of the gate if you do drop the subscription, it will Locke them down even if there is ink in there...
